407.title: Q2: which gods hold the body? breath proves itself by leaving (2)
407.hook: the powers of the body brag that they hold it up, and breath settles the argument by starting to walk out
407.tomorrow: Q3: where does breath come from?
407.howItsDone: Breath (prana) is honored in many Hindu practices, from pranayama in yoga to the five pranas offered with the first mouthfuls of a meal in some traditional households.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first question, and your line, the two paths of the sun. Matter and breath, the moon and the sun. Did your good works and your inner work each get a few minutes? Day four hundred seven.
screen: `THE TWO PATHS OF THE SUN.`

segments.voice: A group project, the night before it's due. Who really carried this? The one who wrote it says the writing. The one who presented says the presentation. The one who booked the room says nobody would've had anywhere to meet. Then the quiet one who did the actual research gets up to leave, and suddenly everyone realizes what they were standing on. Bhargava, from Vidarbha, the second student, asks Pippalada: how many gods hold up a living being? Which of them make it shine? And which one is the greatest? Pippalada answers with exactly that argument.
screen: `WHO REALLY CARRIED THIS?` → `THE QUIET ONE GETS UP TO LEAVE.` → `WHICH GOD IS GREATEST?`

segments.voice: The gods of the body, Pippalada says, are space, wind, fire, water and earth, and speech, mind, the eye and the ear. One day they shine with pride and declare: we hold up this body. We keep it standing. Then breath, prana, the chief of them all, says: don't be deluded. It's me. I divide myself five ways, and I hold it up. They don't believe him. So breath, out of pride, begins to rise, as if to leave. And as he rises, all the others are pulled up with him. When he settles back down, they all settle. The text gives a picture any village would know. When the king bee rises, all the bees rise. When it settles, they all settle. So it was with speech, mind, eye and ear. Then the gods, convinced, sing breath's praises. He burns as fire. He is the sun, the rain, the wind, the earth. He is what is and what isn't, and what never dies. Near the start of this year, in the Chandogya, the powers of the body had the same quarrel, and each one took a turn leaving. Here the story is quicker and sharper. Breath doesn't wait for the others to try. He just begins to stand, and that's enough. Notice what the story is saying about the body. Speech, sight and mind are real powers. But they all ride on something none of them can do without. In the story, nobody notices breath until it starts to go.

segments.voice: Two minutes with the one who holds the house up. Sit, and breathe normally. Then, gently, at the top of an in-breath, pause, just for a moment, nothing strained. See whether everything seems to wait: the thoughts, the listening, even the sense of the room. Then let the breath go on, and feel it all start moving again. Do that two or three times, softly, and then just let breath carry the body without your help. The bell holds the time.
Q2, the second question. Which gods hold the body? Speech, mind, eye and ear all claim it, until breath begins to leave and they all rise with it.

408.title: Q3: where does breath come from? the shadow of the self (3)
408.hook: breath just won the argument; now the third student asks where breath itself comes from, and the answer is a shadow
408.tomorrow: Q4: who sleeps, who dreams, who is awake in sleep?
408.howItsDone: Yoga and Ayurveda teachers still use the names of the five breaths, prana, apana, samana, vyana and udana, from texts like this one, to describe how breath works in the body.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the second question, and your line, when breath left, all left. Did you thank the quiet thing everything depends on? Day four hundred eight.
screen: `WHEN BREATH LEFT, ALL LEFT.`

segments.voice: Breath has just been crowned. Speech, sight, mind: they all depend on it. So the next student, Kausalya, son of Ashvala, does what a good student does after a big answer. He asks the question underneath it. Where is breath born from? How does it come into this body? How does it divide itself, and settle? How does it leave? Pippalada's reply begins with a raised eyebrow. You're asking questions beyond questions, he says. But you are devoted to Brahman, so I'll answer. And the answer starts with something you can see on any sunny sidewalk.
screen: `BREATH HAS BEEN CROWNED.` → `WHERE IS BREATH BORN FROM?` → `QUESTIONS BEYOND QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Pippalada says: breath is born from the self. As a shadow falls from a person, so breath is cast from the self. And it comes into this body, he says, by the working of the mind. Sit with that picture. A shadow is real. It moves, it has a shape, it can cover a whole wall. But it has no life of its own. Take the person away and the shadow goes too. So breath, the king of yesterday's story, turns out to be the self's shadow, close and faithful and completely dependent. Then the text describes how breath runs the body, like a king who tells his officers: you govern these villages, you govern those. The main breath, prana, stays in the eyes and ears, the mouth and nose. Apana, the down-going breath, works in the lower body. Samana, in the middle, carries the food offered into the body evenly, and from it, the text says, rise seven flames. Vyana moves through the channels that branch out from the heart. And udana, the up-going breath, rises through one channel at the end of life, and carries a person on, to a good world for good deeds, a painful one for wrongs, and back to the human world for a mix of both. Outside the body, the text says, the rising sun is breath too, and the power in the earth steadies the down-going breath. So, back to Kausalya's question beyond questions: where does breath come from? From the self, the way a shadow comes from a person. Tomorrow's student follows that self into sleep.

segments.voice: Two minutes with breath as a shadow. Sit, and watch the breath move, the way you'd watch your shadow walk beside you. It goes where you go. It changes shape. Now, gently, turn toward what the shadow falls from: the stillness that's aware of breathing, before any breath begins. You don't have to find it. Just face that way, and let the breath keep moving on its own, close and faithful. The bell holds the time.
Q3, the third question. Where does breath come from? From the self, Pippalada says, as a shadow falls from a person, and it enters the body by the working of the mind.

409.title: Q4: who sleeps, who dreams, who is awake in sleep? (4)
409.hook: the fourth student asks about bedtime: when you sleep, what goes to sleep, what dreams, and what stays awake?
409.tomorrow: Q5–6: om, and the person of sixteen parts
409.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often read the Prashna's fourth question alongside the Mandukya's teaching on waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and use sleep as a daily example of awareness that continues without the senses.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the third question, and your line, as a shadow. Breath, cast from the self the way your shadow is cast from you. Did your shadow remind you? Day four hundred nine.
screen: `AS A SHADOW.`

segments.voice: Last night, you did something remarkable and you don't remember it. You lay down, and the room went away. Then, maybe, you were somewhere else entirely, talking to someone who's been gone for years, in a house that doesn't exist. Then nothing at all, for a while. And then you woke up and you were you again, with no gap in who you are. Gargya, the fourth student, asks about exactly that. What is it in a person that sleeps? What stays awake? Which god sees dreams? Whose is the happiness of deep sleep? And on what does everything rest?
screen: `THE ROOM WENT AWAY.` → `A HOUSE THAT DOESN'T EXIST.` → `WHAT STAYS AWAKE?`

segments.voice: Pippalada starts with a sunset. As the rays of the setting sun all gather back into its disk, and spread out again when it rises, so, when a person sleeps, all the senses gather into the mind. Then that person doesn't hear, see, smell, taste, touch, speak or walk. People say: they're asleep. But not everything sleeps. The fires of breath, Pippalada says, stay awake in this city of the body, tending it all night, like the household fires of a sacrifice. Then dreams. In a dream, the mind, the god of the senses, experiences its own greatness. What it has seen, it sees again. What it has heard, it hears again. Things seen and unseen, heard and unheard, real and unreal, it sees them all. Then deep sleep. When the mind is overcome by light, it sees no dreams, and a happiness rises in the body. And at last, an image: as birds go to a tree to rest, so everything goes to rest in the highest self. Then comes the answer to the last question, what everything rests on. This one, the text says, is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, the doer, the person who is understanding itself. And that one rests in the highest, imperishable self. So who is awake in sleep? Breath, keeping the house. And under it, the one who sees, which never needed eyes to begin with.
screen: `THE SENSES GATHER, LIKE THE SUN'S RAYS.` · `THE FIRES OF BREATH STAY AWAKE.` · `IN DREAMS, THE MIND SEES ALL.` · `BIRDS COME HOME TO A TREE.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO SEES.`

segments.voice: Two minutes like the setting sun. Sit, eyes closed, and let the senses gather in. Let sounds go a little farther off. Let the body's edges soften. Notice the mind still making pictures, the way it does at the edge of sleep. Let them come and go. Under it all, the breath keeps going, by itself, like a fire someone else is tending. Rest there, like a bird come home to a tree, and notice that something is still watching, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Q4, the fourth question. Who sleeps, who dreams, who is awake in sleep? The senses sleep in the mind, the mind dreams, breath keeps watch, and the seer rests in the highest self.

410.title: Q5–6: om, and the person of sixteen parts (5–6)
410.hook: the last two students ask about om and about a person made of sixteen parts, and one of them admits he once had to say, I don't know
410.carry: the sixteen parts return to the sea
410.howItsDone: Om is commonly chanted at the start and close of Hindu prayer and study, and some teachers use the Prashna's line about a lie drying a person up to the root when they speak about truthfulness.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-TEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fourth question, and your line, the one who sees. Did you say goodnight to the one who sees? Today, the last two questions, and the end of the Prashna. Day four hundred ten.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SEES.`

segments.voice: Sukesha, the sixth student, opens with a story against himself. A prince of Kosala once came to me, he says, and asked: do you know the person of sixteen parts? I said, I don't know. If I knew, why wouldn't I tell you? And then he added something you don't often hear from a student: whoever speaks what isn't true dries up to the root. So I can't speak falsely. The prince got into his chariot without a word, and left. Now, Sukesha says to Pippalada, I'm asking you. Where is that person?
screen: `DO YOU KNOW THE SIXTEEN PARTS?` → `I DON'T KNOW.` → `A LIE DRIES UP TO THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: First, the fifth question, from Satyakama. What does a person win who meditates on om until the end of life? Pippalada says om is both the higher and the lower Brahman, and its sounds open different worlds. Meditate on one of its three sounds, and you come quickly back to the human world. On two, and you go to the world of the moon, and return. But one who meditates on all three, the whole of om, he says, is freed from wrong the way a snake slips out of its old skin. Then Sukesha's question. Where is the person of sixteen parts? Right here, Pippalada says, inside the body. And he tells how the sixteen arise. The self thought: when I leave, who will leave with me? It made breath. From breath, faith. Then space, wind, light, water, earth, the senses, mind and food. From food, strength. Then discipline, sacred verses, action, the worlds, and finally, name. Sixteen. Everything a life is made of. Then an image. As rivers flowing toward the sea reach it and disappear, their names and shapes broken up, and people simply say, the sea, so these sixteen parts, flowing toward the person, reach it and disappear. Their names are gone. People simply say, the person. And that one is without parts, and deathless. The six students, the text says, honored Pippalada and said: you are our father, who carries us across our ignorance to the farther shore. Six questions began with a teacher saying, if we know. They end with students saying, thank you.
screen: `OM: THE HIGHER AND THE LOWER.` · `LIKE A SNAKE OUT OF ITS SKIN.` · `SIXTEEN PARTS, FROM BREATH TO NAME.` · `RIVERS REACH THE SEA AND LOSE THEIR NAMES.` · then, large: `THE PERSON WITHOUT PARTS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the list of sixteen. It starts with breath and ends with name. Sit, and begin where the list begins: one breath in, one breath out. Then let a few of the others pass through your attention, in no hurry: faith, the space around you, the warmth of the body, the food you ate today, the work of your hands. Last of all, your name. Don't hold on to any of it. Then come back to the first one, the breath, and stay there. The bell holds the time.
Q5 and 6, the last two questions. Om opens the higher and lower worlds; the person of sixteen parts is right here, and the parts return to it like rivers to the sea.

411.title: The two knowledges — lower (the Vedas) and higher (that by which the imperishable is grasped) (1.1)
411.hook: a great householder asks for the one thing that, once known, makes everything known, and hears that even the Vedas count as the lower knowledge
411.howItsDone: In traditional Vedic schools students still memorize the Vedas and study the six auxiliary sciences, the vedangas, and Vedanta teachers use the Mundaka's two knowledges to explain why study is a ladder rather than the goal.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Prashna's last questions. Your line was the sixteen parts return to the sea. Did you say I don't know, plainly, when you didn't? Today, the Mundaka Upanishad begins. Day four hundred eleven.
screen: `THE SIXTEEN PARTS RETURN TO THE SEA.`

segments.voice: A library with every book ever written. A whole lifetime in it might get you through one shelf. Then someone walks in and asks the librarian: is there one thing I could know, and then everything else would make sense? That's how the Mundaka Upanishad opens. A man named Shaunaka, a great householder, comes properly, as a student should, to the sage Angiras. And he asks: Sir, what is it that, when it is known, all of this becomes known? And Angiras's answer starts by dividing every kind of knowing in two.
screen: `A LIBRARY OF EVERY BOOK.` → `ONE THING THAT MAKES SENSE OF ALL?` → `SHAUNAKA ASKS ANGIRAS.`

segments.voice: The Mundaka belongs to the Atharva Veda, and it opens with its own family tree. Brahma, first of the gods, taught this knowledge to his eldest son, Atharvan. Atharvan passed it on, teacher to student, down to Angiras. Then Shaunaka asks his question, and Angiras says: two knowledges are to be known, so say those who know Brahman. The higher, and the lower. Then the surprise. The lower knowledge is the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva Veda. And with them, phonetics, ritual, grammar, the study of words, meter and astronomy, the six sciences that serve the Vedas. All of it: lower. And the higher? That by which the imperishable is grasped. Akshara, the imperishable, the one that doesn't wear away. Notice where this is said. Not by a critic outside the tradition. Inside the Atharva Veda itself, the Veda calls its own recitation the lower knowledge. Shankara reads the lower as knowledge of words and rites, and the higher as the direct knowing that the words point to. No one in the story throws the Vedas away. Shaunaka learned them. Angiras learned them. They're the ladder you climb, and the Upanishad is part of the Veda too. The point is about what kind of knowing it is. You can know everything about a mango, its region, its chemistry, its price, and never have tasted one. The lower knowledge is everything about. The higher is the taste. And Shaunaka's question, what makes everything known, has only one kind of answer.
screen: `WHAT, ONCE KNOWN, MAKES ALL KNOWN?` · `TWO KNOWLEDGES: HIGHER AND LOWER.` · `EVEN THE FOUR VEDAS ARE THE LOWER.` · `THE HIGHER GRASPS THE IMPERISHABLE.` · then, large: `PARA AND APARA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of the two knowledges. Think of something you know a lot about: a song, a recipe, a person. Run through the facts you know. Then set the facts aside and remember what it's actually like: the taste, the sound, the feel of being with them. Notice the difference. Then, if you'd like, turn toward this moment the same way. Not facts about it. Just what it's like, right now, to be here. The bell holds the time.
The two knowledges. In the Mundaka, the lower is the Vedas and their sciences; the higher is that by which the imperishable is grasped.

412.title: The spider and the web; the hair on the body; the plants from the earth (1.1)
412.hook: how does one imperishable thing become a whole world? the Mundaka answers with three pictures from any backyard
412.howItsDone: The spider verse of Mundaka 1.1.7 is a standard teaching text in Vedanta, and teachers of different schools explain it in class to show how they understand the relation between Brahman and the world.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the two knowledges, the lower that knows about, the higher that grasps the imperishable. Did you catch yourself knowing all about something you hadn't tasted? Day four hundred twelve.
screen: `TWO KNOWLEDGES.`

segments.voice: Early morning, a garden. Between two branches there's a web that wasn't there last night, wet with dew, every thread catching light. And somewhere near the middle sits its maker, who brought no materials. No wood, no wire, no thread from a store. The whole thing came out of the spider's own body. Angiras has just told Shaunaka about the imperishable. The obvious next question is how one changeless thing could turn into everything we see. And instead of a theory, the Mundaka gives three pictures. The first is that spider.
screen: `A WEB THAT WASN'T THERE LAST NIGHT.` → `NO MATERIALS BROUGHT IN.` → `THREE PICTURES.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. Yathorna-nabhih srijate grihnate cha. As a spider sends out its thread and draws it back in. As plants spring up from the earth. As hair grows on the head and body of a living person. So, from the imperishable, everything here comes into being. Three pictures, and each one teaches something different. The spider: the world doesn't come from some second stuff outside the source. The web is spun from the spider itself, and it can be drawn back in. The plants: the world rises naturally, the way green comes up after rain, without anybody pushing. And the hair: it grows from a living person without that person thinking about it at all. You don't decide to grow your eyebrows. So the source isn't straining. The world comes out of it the way hair comes out of you. Then the next verses add: through tapas, through that focused heat, Brahman swells, and from it comes food, from food breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and in action, the deathless. And the one who knows all, whose very tapas is made of knowledge, gives rise to name, form and food. Teachers read the spider differently. Advaita teachers say the web is an appearance, and the spider alone is ultimately real. Ramanuja's school reads the world as truly Brahman's own body, real and dependent. Madhva's school reads Brahman as the independent cause of a world that stays distinct from it. All three keep the spider. Even the Sanskrit word is a small picture: urnanabhi, spider, joins urna, thread or wool, and nabhi, navel.
screen: `AS A SPIDER SPINS AND DRAWS BACK.` · `AS PLANTS RISE FROM THE EARTH.` · `AS HAIR GROWS WITHOUT TRYING.` · `SO, FROM THE IMPERISHABLE, ALL THIS.` · then, large: `URNANABHI.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the three pictures. Sit, and feel your breath go out like a thread, and come back in. Out, and drawn back. That's the spider. Then notice something growing in you without your effort: your hair, your nails, the steady beat of the heart. That's the hair. Then let thoughts rise and fall on their own, the way plants come up from the ground, without pushing them. Rest at the center, where the thread comes from. The bell holds the time.
The spider and the web. The Mundaka's picture of a world spun from its own source, as naturally as plants from the earth and hair from a living body.
screen: `THE SPIDER AND THE WEB — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: as the spider. Today, when you see a web, or a plant pushing through a crack, let it remind you of the Mundaka's three pictures. Day four hundred twelve.

413.title: Rituals are leaky boats (1.2)
413.hook: the Mundaka praises the fire rites as true, then calls them unsteady boats, and both statements sit side by side in the same chapter
413.tomorrow: go to a teacher, fuel in hand
413.howItsDone: Hindu households keep daily and seasonal rites, from lighting a lamp to fire offerings (homa), and Vedanta teachers explain this passage as a lesson about what rites can reach, not a call to stop them.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the spider and the web, and your line, as the spider. Did a web or a stubborn plant remind you of the three pictures? Day four hundred thirteen, the end of week fifty-nine.
screen: `AS THE SPIDER.`

segments.voice: A rowboat can be a perfectly good boat. It'll take you around the lake, out to the dock, across to the picnic spot. Now try to cross an ocean in it. Nothing about the boat has changed. What changed is where you're trying to go. The second section of the Mundaka does something bold with that idea. It's talking about the great fire rites of the Vedas. First, it honors them. Then it calls them boats. And then it tells you what kind of boats.
screen: `A GOOD ROWBOAT.` → `NOW CROSS AN OCEAN IN IT.` → `THE RITES ARE BOATS.`

segments.voice: The section opens with a clear yes. This is the truth, it says: the rites the sages saw in the sacred verses are spread out in many ways. Practice them faithfully. This is your path to the world of good deeds. Then it describes the fire offering in loving detail, the seven flickering tongues of flame, each with a name: the black one, the terrible, the swift as thought, the deep red, the smoky, the sparkling, the one of every shape. And then the turn. Plava hy ete adridha yajnarupah. Unsteady, indeed, are these boats, the eighteen forms of sacrifice. Fools who praise them as the highest good go again and again to old age and death. Thinking themselves wise, the text says, they wander around like the blind led by the blind. They enjoy the heaven their good works earned, and then, when it runs out, they come back down. So which is it? Are the rites true or leaky? The Mundaka says both, on purpose. The rites really do what they promise. They earn a good world. But a good world is still a world that ends. They're boats for the lake, not the ocean. And then the line that explains the whole section: the uncreated is not won by what is made. Nasty akritah kritena. Nothing you build, however holy, can build your way to the unbuilt. Different schools weighed this differently. The Mimamsa tradition held ritual itself as the heart of the Veda. Vedanta teachers read this passage as the turn toward knowledge. Others keep the rites and the inner search side by side.
screen: `FIRST: THE RITES ARE TRUE.` · `SEVEN TONGUES OF FLAME.` · `THEN: UNSTEADY BOATS.` · `THE UNMADE ISN'T WON BY THE MADE.` · then, large: `PLAVA HY ETE ADRIDHA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in the boat. Think of one thing you do faithfully, a habit, a ritual, a routine that's good for you. Honor it for a breath: it works, it carries you. Then ask gently: where is it carrying me? And is there somewhere it can't go? Don't answer quickly. Then let the question go and just sit, not doing anything at all for a moment. Nothing made, nothing earned. The bell holds the time.
Rituals are leaky boats. The Mundaka honors the fire rites as true, then calls them unsteady boats: they earn good worlds, but the uncreated isn't won by what's made.
screen: `RITUALS ARE LEAKY BOATS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the boat leaks. Today, keep doing your good routines, and once, ask where you're rowing. And that's week fifty-nine: breath leaves, a shadow, awake in sleep, sixteen parts, two knowledges, the spider, and the leaky boats. Day four hundred thirteen.
